newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Cash woes dog Russian space programme.
newsitem.headline: Cash woes dog Russian space programme.

text.p: Russian space officials said on Monday they hoped the failure of the Mars-96 mission would not doom their cash-strapped but prestigious space programme.
"It's a heavy blow to the whole programme because we don't have another similar project," said Yuri Milov, deputy director of the Russian Space Agency.
The Mars probe, which crashed into the sea on Monday just over a day after liftoff, took off two years late because of a shortage of state funding.
Milov said around $300 million worth of work and equipment had been lost when the stricken probe reentered the earth's atmosphere having failed to break out of Earth's orbit.
He said it was too early to determine the exact cause of the disaster, thought to have resulted from a faulty booster, but other officials said a lack of funding could have played a role.

"I do not think hasty pre-launch tests are to blame for the failure. A shortage of funds in the Russian space industry is more likely," said Dmitry Poletayev, head of the launches department of Russian commercial space organisation Glavkosmos.
Moscow -- which in communist times channelled huge resources into a space race against the United States -- no longer has the means or the motivation to spend fortunes on space exploration.
Russia's space programme is still a source of international prestige and great national pride but funding problems have left their mark on an industry desperately seeking foreign funding.

A lack of cash for supply rockets has delayed supplies to the MIR space station four times this year and left the current three-man Russian-American crew with an awkward problem -- overflowing toilets.

Moscow makes money from sharing its MIR space station with the U.S. -- which does not have one of its own -- and letting a string of countries use the Russian-run Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan to launch their telecommunications satellites.
But few of the funds filter back into the industry, where many workers go without pay for months.

"On November 16, when the probe took off, the people at Lavochkin had not been paid for three months," said Stanislav Kulikov, general constructor at the Lavochkin institute, which designed and built the rocket.
Poletayev pointed out, however, that many Western space programmes are run on commercial lines and said he did not think that the mission's failure would deal a death-blow.

"I do not see a global tragedy for the Russian space industry," he said. "Of course, Western companies will be more cautious after this crash. But it does not mean that they will refuse cooperation with Russia in space industry and exploration."
Milov said Russia was still planning a joint Mars mission with the United States and that those involved would meet again in December.
The agency had been preparing an overhaul with a focus on astrophysics rather than planetary exploration, he said, and the Mars-86 failure would have to be taken into account.
But his boss, Yuri Koptev, told Interfax news agency that he did not rule out a new Russian Mars mission.
"With enough financing, a new cosmic experiment to study Mars could take place around 2000-20001," he said.
The failure came as a blow to national prestige as it followed a successful launch of a U.S. robot voyage to Mars two weeks ago.
But in an apparent bid to massage Russians' wounded pride, state television announced what it called "a sensational discovery, this time by our -- Russian -- scientists."
The scientists had discovered signs of life dating back to before Earth's existence in a meteorite that landed in the 1960s in Kazakhstan, it said, without specifying when the discovery was made.
